results.claim: Finite-sequence survival with unrotatable dominoes is in NP.
results.proof_sketch: A certificate specifies the locking position of each domino. For a fixed board state, legal translations of the current fixed-orientation domino form a directed graph with O(WH) vertices, including any constant-size spawn buffer fixed by the rules. Reachability from spawn to the claimed locking position is checked by graph search; support, loss, placement, and deterministic simultaneous row deletion are then checked directly. A reachable state has a simple path of polynomial length, so paths may alternatively be included in the certificate. Repeating this for every explicitly listed piece takes polynomial time.

results.claim: For row-parallel unrotatable dominoes on an odd-width board, there is a computable linear-size upper bound on the number of pieces that can ever survive.
results.proof_sketch: Track each initial physical row as a token; clearing deletes tokens and introduces empty tokens at the top. Until an initial token clears, its initially occupied cells remain barriers, and every horizontal domino in that token occupies two adjacent cells within one of its initial empty intervals. If those intervals have lengths ℓi,j, the token accepts at most ci=Σj floor(ℓi,j/2) pieces and can clear only if every ℓi,j is even. Let C=Σi ci and let q count initial tokens satisfying that necessary parity condition. A newly introduced empty token has one interval of odd length W, so it can never clear and accepts at most floor(W/2) pieces. Thus at most q clears occur and every play has length at most U=C+q floor(W/2). Moreover C≤H floor(W/2) and q≤H, so U≤H(W−1). The quantities are computable in O(WH) time.

results.claim: On an even-width board, two initially empty top rows suffice for survival of arbitrarily many row-parallel unrotatable dominoes.
results.proof_sketch: Partition the columns into fixed adjacent pairs. At the start of a phase, the top two rows are empty. Straight-drop one domino into each pair. Absent an earlier clear, this makes the two column tops in every pair equal, all no higher than the second-highest row. Let T be the greatest pair top and stack dominoes on lower pairs until all reach T. The untouched top row provides lateral access throughout. If no row cleared earlier, row T is now full and clears. If any row clears earlier, end the phase immediately. In either case, the old empty top row shifts down while a new empty row enters, restoring two empty top rows. Every phase uses finitely many pieces, produces at least one clear, and restores its invariant, so phases can be repeated indefinitely.

results.claim: The maximum survival length on an initially empty odd-width W×H board with row-parallel unrotatable dominoes is exactly H floor(W/2).
results.proof_sketch: Every horizontal placement changes one row's occupancy by two. Starting from empty, an odd-width row therefore cannot become full, so no row ever clears. Each row contains at most floor(W/2) disjoint dominoes, giving the upper bound. For W≥3, every edge of the W-vertex odd path belongs to a maximum matching: after choosing that edge, maximum matchings of the two residual subpaths give floor(W/2) edges altogether. Choose one containing the fixed spawn pair and fill it level by level. On the top level, place matching edges farthest-to-nearest on each side and the spawn pair last, preserving travel from spawn. This places H floor(W/2) pieces and leaves one empty cell per row. For W=1, no domino fits and both sides of the formula are zero.

results.claim: The row-capacity bound is not sufficient, and clearing one row does not guarantee indefinite unrotatable-domino survival.
results.proof_sketch: For the 3×3 board top/middle/bottom = .../.#./..., C=2, q=0, and U=2. Both horizontal positions contain the middle column, so the first piece must lock in the top row. Either possible placement intersects every width-three spawn pair, preventing a second piece; the true maximum is one. For the 3×2 board .../..#, placing a domino in the other two bottom cells completes and clears that row. The resulting empty 3×2 board accepts exactly two further pieces by the empty odd-width theorem. Thus the original board survives three pieces but not four, even though its first move clears a row; here C=2, q=1, and U=3.

results.claim: Two initially empty top rows cannot in general be weakened to one on even-width row-parallel boards.
results.proof_sketch: Use the 4×2 board top/bottom = ..../#... and the centered spawn pair in columns 2–3. The first domino either locks at bottom columns 2–3, giving ###.; locks at bottom columns 3–4, giving #.##; or moves left and locks at top columns 1–2 because the filled bottom-left cell blocks descent. The last choice already blocks the next spawn. In either bottom-row choice, no adjacent empty bottom pair remains, so a second domino must lock in the top row. Every horizontal edge of a four-cell row intersects the centered spawn pair, so that second lock blocks the third spawn. Two placements are attainable, but three are not; hence one empty top row does not ensure indefinite survival.

results.claim: For odd-width row-parallel instances whose completely empty initial rows form a top prefix, finite clearing polynomial-time many-one reduces to finite survival.
results.proof_sketch: Let m=floor(W/2), let R be the nonempty initial row tokens, and put K0=Σi∈R ci. A clearing play is impossible if some initial empty run in R is odd or if its given sequence length K differs from K0: every token in R must be tiled and cleared, while an initially empty or newly introduced odd-width token can never clear after receiving a horizontal domino. Map such immediate NO cases to a fixed NO survival instance. Otherwise map (B,K0) to survival on the same board for L=K0+Hm pieces. If B clears, append the empty-board construction of Hm pieces. Conversely, because all empty initial rows are above R, the token bound is U=K0+Hm=L. Reaching L forces every token in R to clear. Delete from that play every placement in an initially empty or newly introduced token. Those tokens always stay above R, so deleted cells supported no retained lock; removing obstacles preserves each retained path. The remaining K0 placements clear R and leave all other tokens empty. The mapping and its parameters are computable in O(WH).

final_writeup:
Six audited claims remain unchanged; the refuted initially empty-board claim is repaired by restoring its row-parallel hypothesis. They give a rigorous partial classification under the source rules. For arbitrary finite sequences, survival is in NP: lock coordinates are polynomial certificates because reachability of each fixed-orientation domino is graph reachability on O(WH) translations.

For the all-horizontal (row-parallel) subfamily, board-width parity produces a strong dichotomy. At odd width, following physical row tokens gives the computable bound U=C+q floor(W/2)≤H(W−1). New empty rows can never clear, because horizontal placements change a row's occupancy by two while W is odd. The initially empty odd board has exact maximum H floor(W/2). This formula is false without the all-horizontal qualifier: on an empty 3×3 board, fixed vertical dominoes locked in columns 1, 3, and 2 fill and simultaneously clear the bottom two rows, returning to the empty board, so the three-piece cycle repeats indefinitely. At even width, two empty top rows support a repeatable clearing phase and hence survival of every finite suffix. The new 4×2 witness ..../#... shows that the two-row premise is real: with a centered spawn, one empty top row allows exactly two placements, not infinitely many. The earlier width-three examples separately show that token capacity need not be reachable and that even a first-move clear need not imply indefinite survival.

There is also a restricted complexity bridge. On an odd-width row-parallel board whose completely empty initial rows form a top prefix, let K0 be the sum of interval capacities over nonempty initial rows. Clearing is immediately impossible unless every such interval has even length and the clearing sequence has length K0. In the remaining cases, clearing reduces to asking whether the same board survives K0+H floor(W/2) pieces. A clearing play extends by the exact empty-board construction. In the reverse direction, surviving that many pieces saturates the token bound and forces every nonempty initial token to clear. Placements made in empty-origin tokens can be deleted: these tokens stay above all nonempty initial tokens, so they never supply support, and deleting obstacles cannot invalidate a retained route. This yields a polynomial many-one reduction. The top-prefix qualification is necessary for this proof; an empty row below filled cells can be used as scaffolding.

This does not yet settle the requested classification. The source's cited hardness of unrotatable-domino clearing is not shown here to satisfy the odd-width, row-parallel, top-prefix promise needed by the new reduction, so it would be invalid to infer NP-hardness. Nor does the linear odd-width bound remove exponentially many placement choices, and arbitrary even-width starting boards remain untreated. If the input formalism permits horizontal and vertical fixed orientations in one sequence, only the NP upper bound applies without further work. No polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hardness reduction covers the full target, so the resolution remains PARTIAL.
